devices._comment: One entry per device. password_env names an environment variable to read the password from at runtime — never put a plaintext password in this file. secret_env is the same idea for the enable/privileged-mode secret — optional, only needed if this account doesn't already log in at privilege 15 (Cisco/Arista-family devices only; ignored on VyOS/Junos, which have no enable-mode concept). Without it, a login that lands in user EXEC ('>') will fail privileged-only commands like 'show running-config' with '% Invalid input detected' — watch for a WARN-level 'could not enter privileged/enable mode' log line at connect time if that happens. port/timeout_seconds/fast_cli/global_delay_factor are optional (defaults shown here). If you see a Netmiko 'Pattern not detected' error, the device is slower to respond than expected (common for a device reached over the public internet rather than a LAN) — raise BOTH timeout_seconds (e.g. 60) and global_delay_factor (e.g. 2) for that device; timeout_seconds alone only covers the initial connection and each command's read timeout, not Netmiko's internal pattern-detection delays that global_delay_factor scales.

detection_rules._comment: Toggle individual rules on/off without editing rules.json. A rule id absent from this map defaults to enabled — every rule below is listed explicitly so this block doubles as a reference of what's available.

ai._comment: Forensicator AI is OFF by default. Set enabled=true and point base_url/model at a local LLM (e.g. Ollama) or a commercial API to get a per-finding verdict written into each finding's ai_analysis field, shown in reports/index.html and printed to the console as each finding is analyzed. Same provider/config shape as the Windows/Linux/macOS collectors: provider: ollama | openai | openai_compatible | azure_openai | anthropic. api_key is only needed for openai/openai_compatible/azure_openai/anthropic. max_evidence_rows caps how much of a large finding's evidence (e.g. a full running-config) is actually sent to the LLM per call.

baselines._comment: Baselines for all 20 rules (rules/rules.json, each rule's baseline_required flag). All optional — an unpopulated key just means that specific rule finds nothing to compare against; see rules/engine.py's module docstring for exactly how each of the two rule families (presence-type vs. pure-diff vs. allowlist-membership) behaves when its baseline here is empty. Populate these gradually as you review real findings from your fleet, not all at once before first use.

expected_local_users._comment: Baseline allow-list for the unauthorized-local-accounts rule. Any local-account line found in running-config not in this list is flagged per device (device_overrides can extend/replace the global list for one host).

threat_intel._comment: Feeds the transit-known-malicious-destination rule (checks a device's NAT/conntrack session table against known-bad IPs — see README's Detection Rules section). Same fetch-with-local-fallback pattern as the Windows collector's hash_source/url_source: at startup, each malicious_ip_sources URL is tried in order until one succeeds and the result is cached to malicious_ips_cache_file; if every URL fails (or malicious_ip_sources is empty), whatever's already in the cache file is used as-is, however stale. The default source below (Feodo Tracker's base ipblocklist.txt, NOT the 'recommended' variant, which is no longer maintained) and the FireHOL fallback are best-effort — verify they're still live for your environment; nothing here fetches on every single run, only when the cache is missing or older than malicious_ip_max_age_days.
